idiom_name: function-pointer struct with an explicit context (closure emulation)
implementation_notes: C has no closures, so a combinator value is a small struct holding a function pointer plus the state it needs (`typedef struct { int (*fn)(void *ctx, int x); void *ctx; } fn_t;`); primitives are ordinary C functions lifted into that struct and combiners (and_then, or_else, many) allocate a fresh struct whose callable closes over the two operands. Where the state can be threaded instead of captured, prefer the classic C user-data parameter (`qsort_r`-style `void *arg`) over a struct - the struct form is only needed when the combinator value itself must be stored and passed around. The classic hand-written structure is always the form here; what a library can add is an arena and a uniform calling convention.
pitfalls: Closure environments need storage: capturing a local by address leaves a dangling `ctx` once the creating frame returns; copy the state into the struct's allocation instead.
Every combiner allocates, so a library without an arena or an explicit destroy protocol leaks on each combine and on each call that builds a temporary.
Thread-safety is per closure: a shared context mutated by combiners is a data race unless the contract makes the callable pure or the context immutable.
Function pointer types must match exactly; a combinator specialised for `int(int)` cannot be reused for another payload size, so libraries lift the payload to `void *` and lose type safety.
